# context-guard An OpenCode plugin that says, once per threshold, how large a session's context has grown and what one more turn on that model now costs. The number it watches is `input + cache.read` from each `session.step.ended`. The whole window is re-sent on every turn, so a long session pays for its own history over and over — and that, not the volume of output, is what quietly empties a subscription or a credit balance. A session that reaches 200k tokens and then runs for another two hundred turns bills those 200k tokens two hundred more times. In the sidebar, under the context figure OpenCode already shows: Red and pulsing, and it stays until the context is cleared. On a model that publishes prices the first line also carries what a turn now costs, as `▲ 174k context · ~$0.26/turn`. There is a toast at the moment each threshold is crossed, a line in the transcript, and a desktop notification — all of them optional. ## Install Clone it into the `plugins` directory beside your `opencode.json`: ```sh git clone https://github.com/pierangeloc/opencode-context-guard \ ~/.config/opencode/plugins/context-guard ``` The server half is discovered automatically. For the sidebar, add it to `cli.json` as well: ```jsonc // ~/.config/opencode/cli.json { "plugins": ["./plugins/context-guard"] } ``` Put it in the global config directory rather than a project's, unless you want it in one project only: context size is a property of how you work, not of a repository. ## Settings Press `/context` in a session, or find **Context thresholds** in the palette. ``` Context thresholds · this session Warn at 100k, 150k one notice each, the first time New session at 200k where compacting stops being the advice Notify both Desktop notification on Compact automatically off ctrl+s Edit everywhere instead ``` `ctrl+s` switches between **this session** and **everywhere**. A session's own setting wins; clear it and the session falls back to the global one. Thresholds are typed the way you say them: `150k`, `1.2M`, `150000`, or `60%` for a share of this model's window. `never` turns the last threshold off. Settings live in the server's plugin storage and are shared by every window, so changing a threshold in one TUI applies to the next turn in another. Changing them re-arms the session, so a threshold you have already passed announces once. ### From the config file The same settings can be defaults in `opencode.json`, which is the place to put per-model rules: ```jsonc { "plugins": [ { "package": "./plugins/context-guard", "options": { "warn": [100000, 150000], "clearAt": 200000, "compact": false, "notify": "both", "system": true, "models": { "anthropic/claude-opus-5": { "warn": [80000], "clearAt": 150000 }, "openrouter/some/cheap-model": { "warn": [0.5], "clearAt": 0.8 } } } } ] } ``` Four layers, narrowest last: **session → model → config file → defaults**. Each supplies only the fields it names. - `warn` — thresholds that each produce one notice. A value of 1 or less is a share of the model's window; above 1 it is an absolute token count. - `clearAt` — the last threshold, where the advice becomes "start a new session" rather than "compact". `null` for none. - `notify` — `both`, `chat` (transcript only), `toast` (sidebar and toast only), or `off`. With `off`, auto-compaction still runs if it is on. - `system` — a desktop notification. macOS only; a no-op elsewhere. - `compact` — run `/compact` for you at the last threshold. - `models` — keyed by `providerID/id`, or a bare `id` to catch the same model however it is routed. ### Choosing thresholds The defaults — 100k, 150k, 200k — are a starting point, not a recommendation. Pick them from how you work: the useful question is not what fraction of the window is full, but how many more turns you expect to take at this size. Window share is a poor unit for this. 137k tokens is 14% of a 1M window and is still re-read in full on every turn: around $0.21 a turn on a frontier model against $0.04 on a mid-sized one. That is why the notice prints the share last and in brackets, where it cannot undercut the warning, and why the thresholds are absolute token counts by default. Cost is reported at list price from the model's published `cost`, picking the right tier for how full the window is — a tier's `size` is the floor it applies *above*, so a 200k tier is the price of everything past 200k. Subscription providers publish no prices, so there the notice simply says nothing about money. ## Scope - Subagent sessions are ignored. They carry their own context, die with their task, and cannot be cleared by hand. - Thresholds re-arm after a compaction, since compaction empties the window. - Each location loads its own instance of the server half, and the event stream is shared between them, so events are filtered by location. Without that a session announces once per project you have open. ## Layout ``` src/guard.ts the arithmetic: thresholds, tiers, prices, parsing. No OpenCode import, so `node --test` covers it and both halves share it src/rpc.ts the settings contract between the two halves src/index.ts server: decides, announces, serves and stores the settings src/tui.tsx terminal: the sidebar line, the toast, the /context dialog index.ts re-export, so a local directory install resolves tui.tsx the same, for the terminal half ``` ```sh node --test test/ ``` Two things about loading a plugin from a local directory, neither of which costs anything to get right but both of which fail quietly: - The directory's **root** `index.ts` and `tui.tsx` are what a local install resolves; the `exports` map in `package.json` is used when it is installed as a package. Having both means one tree works either way. - Relative imports need their **extension**, including `.tsx`. Without it the loader looks for `./src/tui.ts`, does not find it, and the terminal half is simply absent. The failure appears in the client log as `plugin operation failed ... stage=read`, not in the terminal. To confirm the terminal half is loaded, watch the plugin count: ```sh grep 'reconciliation completed' ~/.local/share/opencode/log/opencode.log | tail -1 ``` It goes up by one when the plugin loads, and a load that does real work takes milliseconds rather than microseconds. The TUI picks up changes without a restart. ## License MIT
